nameStory: The genus name Xylographa comes from Greek words meaning 'wood writer' — a perfect description for these lichens that create script-like marks on tree bark. The species name trunciseda refers to its truncated or cut-off appearance, as if someone stopped writing mid-sentence on the bark.
description: **Note: Information about this species is limited and should be verified by experts.** Xylographa trunciseda appears to be a crustose lichen that forms thin, script-like patterns on tree bark. Like other members of its genus, it likely creates dark, linear markings that resemble ancient writing or scratches etched into the bark surface. These lichens are typically quite small and easily overlooked, forming patches just a few centimeters across.

idTips.label: Script-like markings
idTips.description: Look for thin, dark lines that zigzag across bark like mysterious writing — they feel smooth to the touch and are embedded in the bark surface

idTips.label: Bark habitat
idTips.description: Found exclusively on tree bark, never on rocks or soil — the surface feels firm and integrated with the bark texture

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: Markings appear black to dark brown, contrasting sharply with lighter bark — they don't rub off when touched gently

idTips.label: Linear pattern
idTips.description: Forms elongated, narrow lines rather than circular patches — the lines may branch or connect like a network of cracks

funFact: **This fact requires verification.** Wood-writing lichens like Xylographa may actually help protect trees by creating a thin barrier layer on bark surfaces — nature's own form of protective coating that happens to look like ancient hieroglyphics!
confusionNotes: **Confusion species uncertain due to limited information.** Might be confused with bark cracks, insect damage, or other crustose lichens that form linear patterns. Unlike physical damage to bark, lichen markings feel smooth and integrated with the bark surface rather than raised or depressed.
